sentences.text: The holotype consists of an almost complete skeleton of a subadult individual that is flattened.
The cervical vertebrae are short and wide.
The humerus is robust and elongated, measuring 27 millimeters in length.
The ulna is 35.5 millimeters long.
The metacarpals are short, measuring seven millimeters for the first three and 9.3 millimeters for the fourth wing finger metacarpal.
The first phalanx of the wing finger is 44.5 millimeters long, while the second is 35.6 millimeters long.
The first three fingers are well developed and bear short but sharp claws.
The fifth toe is elongated.
The preserved tail length is five centimeters, though part of this is attributed to a section likely added to increase the fossil's value.
A second juvenile specimen proved that an elongated tail was present, though not as long as the falsified tail of the holotype, measuring about 85% of the femur length.
The holotype specimen GMV2128 was discovered around 1995 and obtained by scientists from illegal fossil dealers.
The genus was originally named Dendrorhynchus in 1998 by Ji Shu'an and Ji Qiang but was renamed Dendrorhynchoides in 1999 because the original name was preoccupied by a protozoan named in 1920.
It was not until 2000 that Dendrorhynchoides was identified as an anurognathid, and it was confirmed that the fossil had been retouched before its description.
A juvenile specimen believed to be Dendrorhynchoides was recovered in 2010 from the Middle Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation.
Researchers postulated that Dendrorhynchoides was a tree-dwelling insectivore.
Researchers assumed Dendrorhynchoides had forward-facing large eyes and dark coloration to ambush insects nocturnally like modern nightjars or bats.
Dendrorhynchoides is classified as a genus of anurognathid pterosaur.
The parent group of Dendrorhynchoides is Anurognathidae, and it belongs to the family Anurognathidae.
Dendrorhynchoides is classified in the class Reptilia.
The original authors classified Dendrorhynchoides as a long-tailed rhamphorhynchid rather than an anurognathid due to its presumed long tail.
A 2021 phylogenetic analysis placed Dendrorhynchoides within the subfamily Anurognathinae.
A 2006 phylogenetic analysis by Lü Junchang identified Dendrorhynchoides as the sister taxon to the clade formed by the other two species of Asiaticognathidae.
The fossil range of Dendrorhynchoides spans from the Middle Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, living from the Bathonian to the Aptian stages, between 168.2 and 119.57 million years ago.
Dendrorhynchoides fossils are found in the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation in Liaoning and the Middle Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation in Hebei, China.
The type species D. curvidentatus is likely from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation in Liaoning Province, China.
The holotype specimen is dated to approximately 124.6 million years old.
The holotype of the type species was found in the Jianshangou Bed of the Yixian Formation, dating to 124.5 million years ago.
In 2012, researchers David Hone and Lü Junchang suggested the holotype might actually come from Middle Jurassic deposits rather than the Early Cretaceous.
In a 2020 paper, David Hone reversed his earlier opinion and considered the holotype to be from the Early Cretaceous.

While the holotype's tail was altered by collectors to include a piece of a dromaeosaurid tail, a second juvenile specimen proved that an elongated tail was present, though not as long as the falsified tail of the holotype, measuring about 85% of the femur length.
